articles.title: Intelligence predicts charitable giving and voting in massive Swedish study
articles.summary: A massive analysis of Swedish administrative records reveals that higher cognitive abilities strongly predict prosocial behaviors. Individuals with higher general intelligence are consistently more likely to donate to charity, vote in elections, and buy environmentally friendly vehicles.

articles.title: Your posture may change how much pain you feel
articles.summary: There may be a physical reason lying down feels good when you’re hurting. Pain sensitivity was modestly lower while lying flat, possibly because more blood returns to the chest and activates the body’s pressure sensors.

articles.title: Does a Flux-Defined Markov Blanket Screen Self-Replicating Gray--Scott Spots? A Computational Test of a Blanket Condition from the Free Energy Principle
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.27235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Friston's free energy principle holds that a system separated from its environment by a Markov blanket---a boundary whose states statistically screen its interior from its exterior---can be treated as performing approximate Bayesian inference, and that such blankets arise wherever coupling is short-range. We test this blanket condition in a concrete nonlinear pattern-forming system: self-replicating spots in a reaction-diffusion model that persist, compete, and reproduce. Directed boundary exchange and timescale separation hold up reasonably well

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable
articles.summary: The aging brain may be undergoing a remarkable transformation rather than simply losing its abilities, shifting its focus from remembering details to understanding the bigger picture. Scientists suggest this change could be an evolutionary adaptation that helps older adults develop wisdom and share decades of knowledge with younger generations.

articles.title: Scientists find a way to fight Alzheimer’s brain damage without removing toxic tau
articles.summary: Scientists have found a promising way to protect the brain from Alzheimer’s-related damage by blocking immune cells that contribute to the destruction of neurons. In mice, the treatment preserved roughly 40% more tissue in memory centers and improved memory, even without removing harmful tau protein buildup.

articles.title: Extraversion is linked to faster relief from depressive symptoms
articles.summary: During psychiatric treatment, a patient's personality and depression symptoms change in tandem. A new study reveals that high neuroticism slows recovery across multiple symptoms, while extraversion and agreeableness may help patients bounce back faster.

articles.title: Older adults tell the story of their lives differently, and it may not be a sign of decline, new psychology study suggests
articles.summary: Older adults described both one-time events and recurring routines with more general facts and fewer specific details than younger adults did, yet both age groups struggled similarly when they had to switch between memory types.

articles.summary: A large longitudinal study reveals that early childhood intelligence scores can predict the pace at which gray and white matter develop during adolescence, highlighting distinct patterns of brain refinement and network specialization.

articles.title: One in three teen boys follows Andrew Tate at least a little, and those who do hold more rigid views of manhood
articles.summary: A third of U.S. teen boys in a new survey said they follow Andrew Tate at least a little. Those who did tended to favor emotional detachment, dominance, toughness, and rejecting femininity, even after accounting for their parents' messages.

articles.title: Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find
articles.summary: Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimer’s-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. The strongest benefits appeared at 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps, suggesting that the popular 10,000-step goal may not be necessary.

articles.title: Brain scans map multiple “low road” fear pathways between the human thalamus and amygdala
articles.summary: Animal studies have described “low road” pathways that rush sensory information from the thalamus to the amygdala. A brain imaging study of 113 people now maps several such routes in humans, with some far more consistent than others.

articles.summary: Petting a dog after a stressful task didn’t speed recovery, but in a new experiment it was followed by calmer brain and heart responses when dog owners faced a second stress test soon after.

articles.title: Brain wave study reveals shifting auditory responses in children with ADHD
articles.summary: Children with ADHD process unexpected sounds differently than their peers, but these brain responses change as they grow. New research shows heightened sensitivity to sudden noises in early childhood gives way to blunted responses in middle childhood.
